pipeline.title: Reasoning pipeline

tips.title: Breaks one analysis into 7 visible reasoning steps — each one you can see and challenge, instead of being handed a conclusion.
tips.materials: Lists the facts used, each tagged by reliability (strong/medium/weak/unverifiable); it never fakes what it couldn't verify.
tips.anomaly: Picks the most 'off', highest-explanatory anomaly as the entry point — anomalies are the cracks in a structure.
tips.skeleton: Strips emotion and stance, reducing the event to five neutral elements: subject / object / mechanism / harmed / benefited.
tips.mechanism: Digs the causal chain surface -> deeper -> bottom, down to a transferable underlying structure, and maps the flow of interests.
tips.game: Works out where the players' game settles, and tests the structure against isomorphic cases from other domains.
tips.scenario: Lists key variables and possible branches, each with a probability and observable early-warning signals.
tips.judgment: Gives core judgments with confidence, each carrying a 'falsifiable condition' — what would prove it wrong.
tips.adversarial: Attacks its own conclusion from the strongest opposing view (devil's advocate) and audits its own cognitive biases.

pipeline.disagreeHint: Write an objection or a follow-up question: a rebuttal gets full reasoning for why it's absorbed or held; a question (like "why?") gets a direct answer one layer deeper, not just a verdict on your view.
pipeline.disagreePlaceholder: Rebut: the anomaly entry is wrong; the real key is… / or ask: why does this happen? What's the deeper cause?

action.disclaimer: This page is a self-help reference for thinking and action, not medical, legal, or psychological advice. If self-harm, severe distress, or legal risk is involved, please seek professional and in-person help promptly.

tip.overview: Clear-Actionism is a survival manual for living clearly inside rigid structures: it admits most pain has no built-in meaning and most structures can't be moved, yet refuses passivity and self-deception — change what you can, and regulate what you can't without lying to yourself. It follows the structural analysis, turning 'seeing clearly' into 'being able to act'.
tip.pain: Reframe the emotional pain in your situation into a cooler signal: is it a biological alarm (fear, exhaustion, threat) or a structural signal of being squeezed by some rigid structure? See 'what actually hurts' first, instead of rushing to give it meaning.
tip.triage: Break the situation apart and sort each piece into three buckets: change environment (switch/leave/move/find), change behavior (adjust your own actions or cognition), can't change now (nearly immovable, only regulable). Honest sorting is the precondition for action — don't call the uncontrollable controllable, nor hand the controllable to fate.
tip.selfDeception: Distinguish 'able but idle' from 'truly unable': the former has capacity and room yet uses 'I've seen through it / I don't need it' to mask fear (gently name it); the latter is objectively constrained and deserves empathy, not pushing. A few self-check questions help you look honestly.
tip.minimalAction: Only for the 'change environment / change behavior' parts, give minimal actions you can start today or this week (begin in 5 minutes, iterable). Action produces feedback, and feedback breaks self-deception — start moving, then iterate.
tip.crack: For structures you can't move yet, look for real 'cracks': rule inconsistencies, regulatory gaps, fractures between interests, new technical spaces, usable policies and benefits. This isn't opportunism — it's strategically buying yourself room inside a rigid structure.
tip.placebo: For the parts you truly can't change, use non-self-deceiving regulation (observer practice, physiology first, time-boxed rumination) — these are painkillers, not cures; use them but never mistake them for truth. Close with one principle to settle your mindset.
